aic:36678.texto: Girl with Cherries features a dramatically lit female figure, rendered in loose brushstrokes, emerging from a dark background. Rather than portraying her model as a contemporary woman, Eva Gonzalès dressed her as an 18th-century servant girl, denoted by her frilled linen cap; loose, striped gown; and rolled-up sleeves. Gonzalès, the daughter of an affluent and cultured family, was Édouard Manet’s first and only official pupil, and his influence is particularly clear in this painting: the use of theatrical lighting is reminiscent of his Spanish-style paintings, and the historical clothing reflects his predilection for dressing his models in costumes that suggest other personalities and professions.
aic:36678.title: Girl with Cherries

aic:61741.texto: Professional women artists were rare in the 1730s. The Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, which controlled artistic education and competitive art exhibitions called salons, was closed to women. Instead, artistic careers were traditionally limited to those born into families of artists, who could be trained by a male relative. The subject of this portrait probably belonged to such a clan. The presentation here emphasizes the sitter’s luxurious attire, including a swansdown scarf and a damask morning gown, as well as her vocation: she sits confidently before her easel, her palette in hand.
aic:61741.title: Portrait of an Artist

cma:122341.texto: Like many French portraitists active during the ancien régime, François-Hubert Drouais was skilled at veiling the physical imperfections of his subjects. This portrait certainly has this quality: the face has been idealized, smoothed, and perfected, but the focus of the painting is less on the Marquise and more on her elegant gown, which is a particularly fine rendering of eighteenth-century printed cloth, with the brilliant gold and white fabric strewn with meticulously detailed flowers and lace.

cma:125951.texto: Jean-Marc Nattier was a favorite portraitist of King Louis XV of France. He held the lucrative position as the court painter for Queen Mary Lesczynski, the daughter of the exiled king of Poland. The portrait was long thought to be of Madame Henriette de France, one of the daughters of Louis XV and Queen Mary Lesczynski, but this identification is no longer accepted and the sitter remains unknown. There has been considerable confusion over the identity of many of Nattier's sitters, as they tend to conform to an idealized concept of female beauty.
cma:125951.title: Portrait of a Woman

plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). The presentation here emphasizes the sitter’s luxurious attire, including a swansdown scarf and a damask morning gown, as well as her vocation: she sits confidently before her easel, her palette in hand.

1. **Portrait of a Woman**
   Jean-Marc Nattier · c. 1748 · oil on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1948.183

   Jean-Marc Nattier fue un retratista francés muy solicitado por mujeres aristocráticas, especializado en retratos de mujeres que tienden a un idealizado concepto de belleza femenina. [1] [2]
   El retrato es de una mujer francesa, aunque la identidad exacta de la modelo es desconocida y ha sido objeto de confusión. [2]
   La obra muestra una figura femenina idealizada, lo que corresponde a un retrato de mujer en la pintura francesa.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Though the sitters in his portraits often lack individualized traits, Nattier was fervently sought by French aristocratic women.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1948.183 · CC0 1.0
   [2] “Jean-Marc Nattier was a favorite portraitist of King Louis XV of France. He held the lucrative position as the court painter for Queen Mary Lesczynski, the daughter of the exiled king of Poland. The portrait was long thought to be of Madame Henriette de France, one of the daughters of Louis XV and Queen Mary Lesczynski, but this identification is no longer accepted and the sitter remains unknown. There has been considerable confusion over the identity of many of Nattier's sitters, as they tend to conform to an idealized concept of female beauty.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1948.183 · CC0 1.0

2. **Portrait of the Marquise d'Aguirandes**
   François Hubert Drouais · 1759 · oil on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1942.638

   François-Hubert Drouais fue un retratista francés activo durante el ancien régime, conocido por idealizar y perfeccionar los rostros de sus modelos femeninas. [1]
   El retrato representa a la marquesa d'Aguirandes, una mujer francesa, con énfasis en su vestido elegante y detalles femeninos del siglo XVIII. [1]
   La obra es un retrato femenino francés que destaca la moda y la figura femenina idealizada de la época.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Like many French portraitists active during the ancien régime, François-Hubert Drouais was skilled at veiling the physical imperfections of his subjects. This portrait certainly has this quality: the face has been idealized, smoothed, and perfected, but the focus of the painting is less on the Marquise and more on her elegant gown, which is a particularly fine rendering of eighteenth-century printed cloth, with the brilliant gold and white fabric strewn with meticulously detailed flowers and lace.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1942.638 · CC0 1.0

3. **Girl with Cherries**
   Eva Gonzalès · c. 1870 · Oil on canvas · nineteenth century
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/36678

   Eva Gonzalès, pintora francesa, retrató a una joven mujer vestida como sirvienta del siglo XVIII, con un estilo influenciado por Édouard Manet. [1]
   La obra presenta un retrato femenino francés con una figura femenina iluminada dramáticamente y vestimenta histórica.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Girl with Cherries features a dramatically lit female figure, rendered in loose brushstrokes, emerging from a dark background. Rather than portraying her model as a contemporary woman, Eva Gonzalès dressed her as an 18th-century servant girl, denoted by her frilled linen cap; loose, striped gown; and rolled-up sleeves. Gonzalès, the daughter of an affluent and cultured family, was Édouard Manet’s first and only official pupil, and his influence is particularly clear in this painting: the use of theatrical lighting is reminiscent of his Spanish-style paintings, and the historical clothing reflects his predilection for dressing his models in costumes that suggest other personalities and professions.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/36678 · CC BY 4.0
       “Girl with Cherries”, Eva Gonzalès. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/36678

4. **Portrait of a Woman as Diana**
   Jean-Marc Nattier · 1752 · oil on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1942.643

   Jean-Marc Nattier pintó este retrato de una mujer francesa representada como Diana, diosa de la caza, con atributos mitológicos. [1]
